plain_english: Our philosophers have figured out exactly what you need to learn to argue well. But when it comes to actually using these skills? We're terrible at it. Give any of us an uneducated person to debate, and we don't know what to do with them. As soon as they say something off-topic or confusing, we're lost. We end up insulting them or making fun of them. We say, "This person is ignorant — there's no point trying." But think about a guide who finds someone lost on the road. Does he mock them and walk away? No. He leads them back to the right path. You should do the same thing. Show the uneducated person what's true, and you'll see they can follow along. But if you're not showing them the truth, don't ridicule them. Recognize your own failure instead.
original_excerpt: What things a man must learn in order to be able to apply the art of disputation, has been accurately shown by our philosophers (the Stoics); but with respect to the proper use of the things, we are entirely without practice. Only give to any of us, whom you please, an illiterate man to discuss with, and he cannot discover how to deal with the man. But when he has moved the man a little, if he answers beside the purpose, he does not know how to treat him, but he then either abuses or ridicules him, and says, He is an illiterate man; it is not possible to do anything with him. Now a guide, when he has found a man out of the road, leads him into the right way; he does not ridicule or abuse him and then leave him. Do you also show the illiterate man the truth, and you will see that he follows. But so long as you do not show him the truth, do not ridicule him, but rather feel your own incapacity.

plain_english:
Here was Socrates' greatest and most important trait: he never got angry in arguments. He never said anything mean or insulting. Instead, he put up with people who were being nasty to him and found ways to end the fights. If you want to see how powerful this ability was, read Xenophon's Symposium. You'll see how many arguments he stopped. The poets had good reason to praise this skill so highly:

"Quickly with skill he settles great disputes." Hesiod, Theogony, v. 87.
original_excerpt:
Now this was the first and chief peculiarity of Socrates, never to be irritated in argument, never to utter anything abusive, anything insulting, but to bear with abusive persons and to put an end to the quarrel. If you would know what great power he had in this way, read the Symposium of Xenophon, and you will see how many quarrels he put an end to. Hence with good reason in the poets also this power is most highly praised:

Quickly with skill he settles great disputes. Hesiod, Theogony, v. 87.
